text: Finance teams want invoices paid faster, but cannot hand an AI agent unlimited treasury authority. TallyGuard makes that boundary the product.
A requester starts with an invoice, purchase order, and delivery proof. The system extracts key fields; a person confirms them before the evidence is sealed.
The submitted request gets one traceable ID. Both the requester and finance see its status. Submission alone never releases funds.
Finance reviews the same request. Duplicate evidence, supplier, wallet, timing, and policy are checked. This larger payment needs independent approval.
A separate approver reviews the evidence and records a reasoned decision. The agent can recommend an action, but cannot approve its own exception.
Approval is still not payment. Finance performs the final, separately controlled settlement action. The public website demonstrates this step in simulation mode.
Back in the requester portal, the same ID now shows paid status, the finance note, and a final simulated receipt.
There is also a no-touch path. Finance explicitly versions the policy: fifty USDC per payment and a five-hundred-USDC daily ceiling, subject to treasury headroom and the emergency stop.
Now a forty-USDC request arrives. Its invoice, order, delivery, supplier, wallet, and available budget are checked against that finance-approved boundary.
Because every required control passes and the amount remains inside the limit, the agent settles this simulated request automatically. The requester immediately sees the receipt.
A separate sample queue uses its own policy to show four outcomes: proceed, human review, scheduled, and held. Each decision is explained, and the controls are rechecked before execution.
Compared with fragmented bank handoffs, Circle-controlled wallets and Arc USDC provide an always-on programmable settlement rail. Fiat entry and exit still involve banking partners.
Forty confirmed Arc Testnet transfers. This historical proof is separate from the demo.
TallyGuard: agent speed, finance control, proof on Arc.
